dsmPointer: See DSM-5-TR: Depressive Disorders — Major Depressive Disorder
summary: An episodic condition: for a stretch of weeks, clearly unlike the client's usual self, mood sinks or the capacity for enjoyment drains away, and the body and outlook follow, with changes in sleep, appetite, energy and how the client sees themselves. In session it often shows up as withdrawal and inertia: activity drops, what remains feels less rewarding, and mood sinks further, the loop that behavioral activation targets. Thoughts of death or suicide can be part of the picture. Always ask about past periods of unusually high mood or energy (possible bipolar disorder), and ask directly about suicidal thoughts; this app never rates risk. For clinician review only; this is not a diagnosis.

durationGate.note: Ask whether the low period has been steady rather than a few bad days scattered among good ones. Confirm the required symptom count and timing in DSM-5-TR.

ruleOuts.label: Hypothyroidism
ruleOuts.note: Can cause fatigue, low mood, weight gain, slowed thinking and excess sleep. Consider thyroid testing through the client's medical provider.

ruleOuts.label: Anemia or vitamin deficiencies
ruleOuts.note: Iron, B12 or folate deficiency can cause fatigue, poor focus and low mood. Ask about recent blood work.

ruleOuts.label: Obstructive sleep apnea
ruleOuts.note: Loud snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing and daytime sleepiness suggest a sleep evaluation.

ruleOuts.label: Neurological and other medical illness
ruleOuts.note: Stroke, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, dementia, chronic pain, cancer and post-viral illness can cause or mimic depressive symptoms.

ruleOuts.label: Medication effects
ruleOuts.note: Some medicines, such as corticosteroids, interferon, isotretinoin and certain hormonal treatments, have been linked to mood changes. Review the medication list with the prescriber.

ruleOuts.label: Alcohol, sedative or stimulant effects
ruleOuts.note: Heavy use, intoxication or withdrawal (e.g., a stimulant crash) can produce depressive symptoms. This app does not store substance-use information.

ruleOuts.label: History of manic or hypomanic episodes
ruleOuts.note: Ask about past periods of high energy, little need for sleep, racing ideas or risky spending. Such a history points toward bipolar disorder and changes treatment; refer for psychiatric evaluation.

ruleOuts.label: Bereavement and expected grief
ruleOuts.note: Sadness after a death is expected. In grief the pain is about the loss and tends to ease between reminders. When the low spreads to the client's view of self and future, or suicidal thinking appears, assess for a depressive episode as well.

ruleOuts.label: Psychotic disorders
ruleOuts.note: Hallucinations or delusions that occur outside mood episodes suggest a primary psychotic or schizoaffective disorder.

specifiers.label: Severity: mild, moderate or severe
specifiers.note: Severity sets the ICD-10-CM fourth character (F32.0 to F32.2 or F33.0 to F33.2). Rate it from the whole picture, including how much the client can still manage at work and home; a PHQ-9 trend can support, but not replace, that judgment.

specifiers.label: With psychotic features
specifiers.note: Coded F32.3 or F33.3. Warrants urgent psychiatric referral.

specifiers.label: In partial or full remission
specifiers.note: Coded F32.4 / F32.5 (single episode) or F33.41 / F33.42 (recurrent).

specifiers.label: Single episode vs. recurrent
specifiers.note: Use the recurrent codes (F33.x; ICD-11 6A71) when there has been an earlier, separate episode with a period of improvement in between. See DSM-5-TR for the required interval.

specifiers.label: With anxious distress
specifiers.note: Use when anxiety is a prominent part of the depressive episode itself, not only a separate condition (see DSM-5-TR for the feature list). Linked to higher risk and slower response; screen for anxiety disorders and assess suicidal thinking.

specifiers.label: With mixed features
specifiers.note: Some manic or hypomanic symptoms during a depressive episode. Raises concern for bipolar spectrum illness; refer for psychiatric evaluation.

specifiers.label: With melancholic features
specifiers.note: A severe, 'endogenous'-looking depression: pleasure is all but absent, mood stays fixed whatever happens, and physical and daily-rhythm changes are prominent. See DSM-5-TR for the feature list.

specifiers.label: With atypical features
specifiers.note: Despite the name, a common pattern: mood can still lift for a while when something good happens, and the episode leans toward 'more' rather than 'less' (oversleeping, eating more, a heavy body), often in someone deeply wounded by rejection or criticism. See DSM-5-TR for the feature list.

specifiers.label: With peripartum onset
specifiers.note: Episode begins in pregnancy or soon after the birth (see DSM-5-TR for the time window). Coordinate with obstetric or primary care and screen for risk to the parent and infant.

specifiers.label: With seasonal pattern
specifiers.note: Low periods that follow the calendar, most often arriving in the darker months and clearing as daylight returns. A mood and sleep log kept across the year helps show the pattern.

differentials.label: Persistent depressive disorder (ICD-10-CM title: Dysthymic disorder)
differentials.distinguishing: Low mood has been the client's baseline for years, often described as 'just how I am'; full episodes can sit on top of it. See DSM-5-TR for the duration.

differentials.label: Bipolar II disorder
differentials.distinguishing: A past stretch of hypomania, even a brief or pleasant one the client never saw as a problem, changes the picture. Screen before antidepressants start.

differentials.label: Bipolar disorder, unspecified
differentials.distinguishing: Any history of mania or hypomania that is not yet fully characterized. Refer for psychiatric evaluation.

differentials.label: Adjustment disorder with depressed mood
differentials.distinguishing: Low mood that grew out of a specific recent setback and stays centered on it, without the breadth of a depressive episode.

differentials.label: Prolonged grief disorder
differentials.distinguishing: Grief that has not found a place in the client's life: the person who died still dominates attention and the loss feels unreal or unbearable, well past what the client's culture expects. ICD-11 uses at least 6 months after the death; DSM-5-TR uses about 12 months for adults (confirm the duration in DSM-5-TR). It can co-occur with a depressive episode.

differentials.label: Depressive symptoms due to a medical condition, substance or medication
differentials.distinguishing: Onset and course track the illness, substance or medication. See the rule-out list.

comorbidities.label: Generalized anxiety disorder
comorbidities.note: Depression and GAD often occur together and share poor sleep, fatigue and poor focus. Treat both, and consider GAD-7 alongside PHQ-9.

comorbidities.label: Posttraumatic stress disorder
comorbidities.note: Depression frequently accompanies PTSD and adds to suicide risk. Ask about trauma history.

comorbidities.label: Panic disorder
comorbidities.note: Panic attacks during a depressive episode are linked to more severe illness; assess panic separately.

comorbidities.label: Agoraphobia
comorbidities.note: Staying home may reflect fear-based avoidance rather than low energy; clarify the reason.

comorbidities.label: Alcohol or other substance use
comorbidities.note: Substance use often co-occurs with depression and raises risk. Screen and refer as needed. This app does not store or transmit substance-use information.

interventions.name: Behavioral activation (individual or group)
interventions.evidence: NICE NG222 (2022) lists individual and group behavioral activation among first-line options for less severe depression, and individual behavioral activation for more severe depression. APA Division 12 lists behavior therapy / behavioral activation for depression (check the current rating).
interventions.note: Schedule valued and mastery activities, track mood alongside activity, and reduce avoidance. Works well with an activity log.

interventions.name: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)
interventions.evidence: NICE NG222 lists group or individual CBT for less severe depression, and individual CBT, alone or combined with an antidepressant, for more severe depression.
interventions.note: Targets negative thinking patterns and avoidance. Session count depends on severity.

interventions.name: Interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT)
interventions.evidence: NICE NG222 lists IPT among treatment options for depression.
interventions.note: Focuses on role changes, conflicts, grief and social isolation linked to mood.

interventions.name: Guided self-help
interventions.evidence: NICE NG222 suggests considering guided self-help first for most people with less severe depression.
interventions.note: Uses structured CBT-based materials with brief support sessions.

interventions.name: Group exercise
interventions.evidence: NICE NG222 lists group exercise among options for less severe depression.
interventions.note: Check for medical limits on activity. Choose formats that fit the client's culture, body and budget.

interventions.name: Suicide risk screening and safety planning
interventions.evidence: Clinical standard of care. If PHQ-9 item 9 is above 0 or the client reports suicidal thoughts, follow up with a structured screen (e.g., C-SSRS, link-out only) and safety-planning resources.
interventions.note: The clinician decides on risk level and next steps. Crisis resources (988, local emergency number, findahelpline.com) stay visible on every screen.

interventions.name: Referral for medication evaluation
interventions.evidence: NICE NG222 advises against routinely offering antidepressants first-line for less severe depression unless the person prefers them; for more severe depression a combination of individual CBT and an antidepressant may be offered.
interventions.note: Refer to psychiatry, a primary care provider or a psychiatric nurse practitioner, especially with psychotic features, mixed features, a bipolar history or high risk.

culturalNotes: Many clients, especially from cultures where emotional distress carries stigma, present depression through the body: fatigue, pain, headaches, poor sleep or a 'heavy heart'. Ask about mood and interest directly, in the client's own words.

Idioms such as 'thinking too much', 'nervios' or 'my spirit is tired' may describe depression, anxiety or trauma responses, or none of these. Explore what the phrase means before mapping it to a symptom.
Grief customs and how long mourning is expected to last vary widely. Consider cultural and religious norms before judging grief as prolonged or a depressive episode.

The PHQ-9 has been validated in many languages and countries, but best cut-offs and item performance (e.g., the sleep, appetite and suicide items) can differ across groups and medical settings. Use validated translations and interpret scores with the interview.
Use a trained professional interpreter, not family members, especially when asking about suicidal thoughts.

Religious or spiritual beliefs can be a source of hope and support, and for some clients a source of guilt or stigma about suicide or depression. Explore these respectfully. Use spiritual or faith-integrated approaches only when the client asks for them and after informed consent (see the AACC Code of Ethics for faith-based counselors).

redFlagRules.message: Manic or hypomanic signs are documented in this input: consider bipolar disorder (ICD-10-CM F31.x) rather than unipolar depression, and refer for psychiatric evaluation before starting treatment.

Psychotic symptoms are documented in this input: consider a depressive episode with psychotic features (ICD-10-CM F32.3 / F33.3) or a primary psychotic disorder, and refer for an urgent psychiatric evaluation.
